style: Comprehensive meaningful blend (interpretive prose) + amplified study form; em-dashes used sparingly; narrative register

1.text: In the days when the judges ruled, a famine came over the land. So a certain man of Bethlehem in Judah set out to live for a while in the country of Moab — he and his wife and his two sons.
1.notes: shaphat (H8199) = to judge/govern (the era of Judges). The famine in Bethlehem is bitter irony — Bethlehem means 'house of bread' (beth-lechem), yet there is no bread; so a man of the house of bread goes looking for it in pagan Moab.

2.text: The man's name was Elimelech, his wife's name was Naomi, and his two sons were named Mahlon and Chilion — Ephrathites from Bethlehem in Judah. They came to the country of Moab and settled there.
2.notes: The names carry the story's grief: Naomi (H5281, no'omi) = 'pleasant'; Mahlon (H4248) ≈ 'sickly'; Chilion (H3630) ≈ 'failing/wasting away.'

3.text: Then Elimelech, Naomi's husband, died, and she was left with her two sons.

4.text: They took for themselves Moabite wives — the name of one was Orpah, and the name of the other was Ruth — and they lived there about ten years.

5.text: Then both Mahlon and Chilion also died, and the woman was left bereft of her two children and of her husband — stripped of every man who should have provided for her.
5.amp: ...the woman was left [sha'ar -- left over, a remnant] of her two children and of her husband.
5.notes: sha'ar (H7604) = to remain/be left over. Naomi is reduced to a 'remnant' of a family — in that world, a widow with no sons and no husband had no provider and no future.

6.text: So she set out with her daughters-in-law to return from the country of Moab, for she had heard there that the LORD had visited His people and given them bread.
6.amp: ...the LORD had visited [paqad -- drawn near to attend to, to set right] His people and given them bread [lechem -- bread returns to the 'house of bread'].
6.notes: paqad (H6485) = to visit/attend to, in mercy or in judgment; here in mercy. The first ray of hope: the LORD has come to His people again, and bread has returned to Bethlehem.

7.text: She left the place where she had been living, her two daughters-in-law with her, and they went on their way to return to the land of Judah.

8.text: But Naomi said to her two daughters-in-law, "Go back, each of you, to your mother's house. May the LORD show you covenant kindness, just as you have shown it to the dead and to me.
8.amp: May the LORD deal kindly with you [ya'as hesed -- show you the same loyal, covenant love you have shown], as you have dealt with the dead and with me.
8.notes: hesed (H2617) = loyal, covenant love -- the steady kindness that keeps faith even when no obligation remains. It is the great word of the book; Naomi prays the LORD will repay onto these Moabite women the hesed they have lavished on her own household.

9.text: May the LORD grant that each of you find rest, a home in the house of a husband." Then she kissed them, and they lifted up their voices and wept.
9.amp: May the LORD grant that you find rest [menuchah -- a settled place of security], each of you in the house of her husband.
9.notes: menuchah (H4496) = rest/secure settlement. For a widow, 'rest' meant the shelter of a household -- the very thing Naomi will later seek for Ruth (3:1).

10.text: But they said to her, "No — we will go back with you, to your own people."

11.text: Naomi said, "Turn back, my daughters. Why would you go with me? Do I have more sons in my womb who could become your husbands?
11.notes: Naomi reasons by the law of levirate marriage (Deut. 25:5-10): a widow's brother-in-law was to raise up offspring for the dead. She has no more sons to give -- humanly, she has nothing left to offer them.

12.text: Turn back, my daughters; go your way, for I am too old to belong to a husband. Even if I said, 'I still have hope,' even if I had a husband tonight and bore sons —
12.notes: Naomi presses the hopelessness to its limit: even the most far-fetched scenario could not give Orpah and Ruth husbands in time.

13.text: would you wait for them until they were grown? Would you shut yourselves away from having husbands for them? No, my daughters. It grieves me deeply for your sakes, for the hand of the LORD has gone out against me."
13.amp: ...it is far more bitter for me than for you [mar -- the bitterness she will name herself by, v.20], for the hand of the LORD has gone out against me [His sovereign hand -- she does not doubt that God is behind it all].
13.notes: mar (H4751) = bitter (root of 'Mara,' v.20). Naomi's theology is unflinching: she traces her losses straight to the hand of the LORD -- He is sovereign even over her sorrow.

14.text: Again they lifted up their voices and wept. Then Orpah kissed her mother-in-law goodbye — but Ruth clung to her.
14.amp: ...but Ruth clung to her [dabaq -- held fast, the same word used of a man cleaving to his wife, Gen. 2:24].
14.notes: dabaq (H1692) = to cling/cleave/hold fast. The contrast is the hinge of the chapter: Orpah kisses and leaves; Ruth cleaves and stays. The word is covenant-strong -- the bond of marriage and of loyal love.

15.text: "Look," said Naomi, "your sister-in-law has gone back to her people and to her gods. Go back, after your sister-in-law."
15.notes: Naomi names the real cost of staying: to follow her is to leave Moab's gods for the LORD. The choice set before Ruth is, at heart, a choice of which God she will serve.

16.text: But Ruth said, "Do not urge or press me to leave you behind, or to turn back from following you. For wherever you go, I will go; and wherever you stay, I will stay. Your people will be my people, and your God my God.
16.amp: Do not urge or press me [paga' -- to fall upon, press, entreat] to leave you behind [or to turn from following close behind you]; for where you go, I will go, and where you stay, I will stay [lun -- to lodge, settle for the night, remain] -- your people my people, and your God [Elohim -- the LORD of Israel] my God.
16.notes: Ruth's vow is the heart of the book: a Moabite outsider binds herself by hesed not only to Naomi but to Naomi's God. It is a conversion as much as a kindness -- she forsakes the gods of Moab to take refuge under the wings of the LORD (cf. 2:12).

17.text: Where you die, I will die, and there I will be buried. May the LORD deal with me, be it ever so severely, if anything but death itself parts you from me."
17.amp: May the LORD do so to me, and more also [the full self-imprecating oath formula -- she calls down God's judgment on herself if she breaks faith], if anything but death parts you and me.
17.notes: Ruth seals her pledge with a covenant oath sworn in the name of the LORD -- the God she has just claimed as her own. Her loyalty is now unbreakable, answerable to heaven.

18.text: When Naomi saw that Ruth was resolved to go with her, she said no more to dissuade her.
18.amp: When she saw that she was firmly resolved [amats -- had braced and strengthened herself] to go with her, she stopped urging her.
18.notes: amats (H553) = to be strong/resolute. Ruth has set her face; Naomi's arguments fall silent before such settled love.

19.text: So the two of them went on until they came to Bethlehem. And when they arrived, the whole town was stirred over them, and the women asked, "Can this be Naomi?"
19.notes: hamah (H1949) = to be in commotion/stirred up. Naomi left a wife and mother and returns a widow stripped bare -- so changed that the town can hardly believe it is she.

20.text: "Do not call me Naomi," she told them. "Call me Mara, for the Almighty has dealt very bitterly with me.
20.amp: Do not call me Naomi ['Pleasant']; call me Mara ['Bitter'], for the Almighty [Shaddai] has dealt very bitterly with me [marar -- made my life bitter].
20.notes: Naomi (H5281) = 'pleasant'; Mara (H4755) = 'bitter'; Shaddai (H7706) = 'the Almighty,' the patriarchs' name for the all-sufficient God. She does not curse God -- she confesses Him as sovereign even over the bitterness.

21.text: "I went out full, but the LORD has brought me back empty. Why call me Naomi, when the LORD has testified against me, and the Almighty has brought calamity upon me?"
21.amp: I went out full [a husband and two sons], and the LORD has brought me home again empty; why call me 'Pleasant,' when the LORD has testified against me [anah -- answered/witnessed against me, as in a lawsuit] and the Almighty has afflicted me?
21.notes: 'Full' and 'empty' frame her grief; the irony is that she is not empty at all -- Ruth, worth more than seven sons (4:15), stands beside her, and the LORD is already at work. Naomi sees the hand of God in her loss but not yet His hidden mercy.

22.text: So Naomi returned, and with her Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law, who had come back from the country of Moab. And they arrived in Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest.
22.amp: ...they came to Bethlehem at the beginning of the barley harvest [the season of new grain -- the quiet turn from emptiness toward the LORD's provision].
22.notes: The chapter of famine and death ends on harvest. 'Empty' Naomi has returned to the 'house of bread' just as the barley ripens -- and the reader, unlike Naomi, can already feel the LORD's providence stirring.
